common_name: Council Fire Possumhaw Holly (Heavy-Fruiting Female Deciduous Holly)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Council Fire is a female possumhaw selection and needs a male Ilex decidua such as 'Red Escort' or 'Council Fire's Escort' nearby for reliable berry set.

directions: Council Fire is a heavy-fruiting selection of possumhaw, the native deciduous holly whose leaves drop each fall to leave bare branches thickly studded with bright orange-red berries that persist deep into winter, a striking display in the native shade garden and a valuable food source for overwintering songbirds. It is a female clone and, like all possumhaw, needs a male Ilex decidua growing within pollinating range to set its heavy berry crop. Adaptable to both moist bottomland soils and drier upland sites, it tolerates wetter ground and heavier shade than most hollies, making it useful along a woodland edge or streambank. Prune immediately after the fruit display fades in late winter if shaping is needed, since flower buds for the next season's berries form on new growth soon after.
sources: North Carolina State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
Mississippi State University Extension — Native Hollies

common_name: Evergreen Cutleaf Blackberry (Thorny Parent of Oregon Thornless Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container canes in spring on a trellis in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil; Evergreen is the thorny straight-species parent from which the popular thornless sport 'Oregon Thornless' arose and needs sturdy wire support for its long, arching canes.

directions: Evergreen is a vigorous, heavily thorned blackberry cultivar named for its deeply cut, fern-like leaflets that hold their glossy dark green color later into fall and winter than typical blackberry foliage. It is best known today as the parent from which the widely grown thornless sport 'Oregon Thornless' was selected, but the thorny original is still grown where its notably firm, small-seeded, long-shelf-life berries are valued for processing and jam-making. Train the long, trailing canes onto a sturdy trellis each season, tying in first-year primocanes that will fruit the following summer, and remove spent floricanes after harvest to make room for new growth. Its dense, thorny habit also makes it useful as an impenetrable barrier hedge in addition to its fruiting value.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Growing Blackberries in the Home Garden
Washington State University Extension — Bramble Fruit Production

common_name: Popcorn Miniature Rose (Prolific White Button-Flowered Miniature Rose)

planting.note: Plant container-grown roses in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; Popcorn is the parent cultivar behind the sport 'Gourmet Popcorn' and is itself a heavy, continuous bloomer suited to borders and containers.

directions: Bred by Dennison Morey and introduced in 1974, Popcorn is a classic miniature rose prized for its extraordinary floral display: small, semi-double white flowers with a light yellow base and a sweet, honey-like fragrance smother the compact plant almost continuously from late spring through fall, giving the popcorn-like massed effect that gives the cultivar its name. Its low, mounded, disease-resistant habit suits it to border edging, rock gardens, and container culture equally well. Deadhead spent blooms regularly to encourage continuous rebloom, and provide full sun and good air circulation to keep the abundant foliage healthy through the humid Gulf Coast growing season. It has served as a parent to several popular sports and seedlings, including the golden-yellow 'Gourmet Popcorn'.

common_name: Skyrocket Hybrid Musk Rose (Wilhelm, Deep Red Fragrant Musk Rose)

planting.note: Plant bare-root or container roses in spring in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; Skyrocket (also sold as Wilhelm) is a Kordes hybrid musk from 1934 and the parent cultivar cited in the later introduction 'Will Scarlet'.

directions: Bred by Wilhelm Kordes and introduced in Germany in 1934 under the name Wilhelm, Skyrocket is a hybrid musk shrub rose producing large clusters of semi-double, deep crimson-red flowers with a strong, sweet musk fragrance from late spring through fall. Its vigorous, arching canes can be grown as a large freestanding shrub or trained as a short climber against a fence or pillar, and the color deepens further in cool fall weather. Like other hybrid musks it tolerates a bit more shade than modern hybrid teas and performs well massed in a mixed shrub border. It gave rise to the later, brighter-scarlet sport 'Will Scarlet', still grown today. Prune lightly in late winter to shape and remove dead wood, since hybrid musks bloom best on a framework of older canes rather than hard annual renewal pruning.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring or early fall in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; Flamboyant is the streaked sport cited as a parent of the later introduction 'Shade Fanfare'.

directions: Flamboyant is a streaked sport of the older cultivar Hosta 'Fascination', notable for broad, heart-shaped leaves with a wide, irregular creamy-white center bordered by an uneven dark green margin, a bold variegation pattern that brightens shaded borders and containers. Pale lavender flowers rise on scapes above the foliage in mid-to-late summer, though the plant is grown primarily for its striking leaf pattern rather than its bloom. Like other variegated hosta sports it can occasionally revert to solid green or produce reverted growth, which should be divided out and discarded to keep the clump true to type. It served as a parent in the breeding of the widely grown 'Shade Fanfare'. Grow in humus-rich, consistently moist soil in shade to light morning sun, and divide congested clumps every four to six years in spring.
